newsitem.title: POLAND: ABN-AMRO RECOMMENDS LONG ZLOTY POSITIONS - REPORT.
newsitem.headline: ABN-AMRO RECOMMENDS LONG ZLOTY POSITIONS - REPORT.

text.p: The zloty's future largely depends on a monetary tightening which would improve Poland's current account but the outlook for the currency is positive, a senior ABN-Amro analyst said in a Thursday report.

Tony Norfield, head of the bank's London treasury research said the zloty was less at risk from the widening trade gap than the Czech koruna because Poland's growth has been stronger and high yields were more sustainable.

Earlier this year the Czech Republic had to devalue its currency after foreign investors began winding up their large short-term koruna positions on the fast growth of the current account deficit and slowed economic growth.
"We would recommend long zloty positions, since the high yields give forward points that project a (zloty) depreciation faster than is likely," Norfield said.

"However, it is important that the new government shows its commitment to fiscal tightening so as not to question longer-term financial viability," he said. Poland is scheduled to hold parliamentary elections on September 21.

The government wants to cut next year's budget deficit to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product while the central bank and the International Monetary Fund say 1.5 percent is the most Poland can afford before balancing its books in 1999.

Norfield noted the the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of ex-communists and the right wing Solidarity Election Action (AWS) had the biggest chances of winning the elections and becoming the core of the next government.
He said the markets would be concerned if the smaller co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL) or the populist Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP) gained much ground in the polls.
"However, opinion polls indicate that this is unlikely," Norfield said.

Norfield said that in the medium-term foreign direct investment would substantially help finance Poland's current account gap and a temporary current account deficit of some 5-6 percent of GDP was possible without a foreign exchange strain.
"The key issue is whether Polish fiscal and structural policies remain credible, so that foreign direct investment inflows are attracted," Norfield said.

Norfield expected the zloty would close the year at around one percent below the basket of currencies at 3.5200 against the dollar and 2.07 against the mark if the dollar/mark rate returns to the expected 1.7000.
He noted that the zloty's exchange rate against a basket of the dollar and the mark is much more stable than its individual exchange rates against the U.S. and German units.
"Unless one has a firm view on dollar/mark, it therefore makes sense to trade the zloty against a dollar/mark basket, rather than simply against either the dollar or the mark," Norfield said.
The zloty closed at 1.48 percent below parity on Thursday, 3.4560 against the dollar and 1.8820 against the mark.
